title: Complete Redesign of a Complex SaaS Workflow
problem: A multi-step operational workflow — approvals, permissions, offline states — has accumulated a decade of exceptions. Users route around it, and support absorbs the difference.
goal: Redesign the workflow so the common path is obvious and the exceptional paths remain possible, and show the reasoning at every step.
process: Current-state audit → user evidence → information architecture → state machine → permissions model → edge cases → high-fidelity core path.
research: Support ticket taxonomy, session recordings, five user interviews, and a task-completion baseline.
discovery: Where users abandon, where they invent workarounds, and which exceptions are actually the same exception.
ux: IA restructure, a single canonical state machine, progressive disclosure for the exceptional cases, and error states designed rather than defaulted.
metrics: Task completion rate, time-to-complete, support tickets per 100 workflows, and error rate as a guardrail.
tradeoffs: Chose a single opinionated path over configurability. Costs flexibility for the 5% of customers with genuinely unusual processes; buys clarity for the 95%.
risks: Migration for existing customers; the 5% may be commercially significant. Mitigation is an explicit escape hatch, not configurability everywhere.
businessImpact: Modelled: 30% reduction in workflow-related support volume, 20% faster task completion.
rationale: Ranked #1 by the audit because it shows systems thinking, UX and execution simultaneously — all three of your strongest areas, in one public artefact.

title: AI Copilot PRD
problem: Users need answers that live across documentation, historical records and their own data. Search returns links; they need conclusions.
goal: Specify and prototype a copilot that answers grounded questions, shows its sources, and can be evaluated rather than admired.
process: Problem framing → retrieval design → prompt architecture → evaluation harness → staged rollout → unit economics.
research: Query log analysis, ten user interviews, and a taxonomy of question types.
discovery: Which questions users actually ask, and which of those the system should refuse to answer.
ux: Streaming responses, visible sources, explicit uncertainty, and a correction path when the answer is wrong.
metrics: Groundedness score on a 50-case eval set, answer acceptance rate, cost per query, p95 latency, and escalation rate as a guardrail.
tradeoffs: Chose smaller retrieved context with higher precision over large context with higher recall. Costs some coverage; buys trust, latency and margin.
risks: Hallucination on adversarial queries; cost blow-up at scale. Mitigated by the eval set and a hard context budget.
businessImpact: Modelled: 40% deflection of a support category, 15 minutes saved per affected user per week.
rationale: Ranked #2. Covers retrieval, prompts, evaluation, rollout and metrics — and AI product evaluation is on the should-improve list.

title: Marketplace Strategy Document
problem: A two-sided marketplace has healthy demand and constrained supply, and every growth lever it pulls makes the imbalance worse.
goal: Produce a strategy that identifies the real constraint and sequences the interventions that relieve it.
process: Market structure → liquidity analysis → constraint identification → intervention sequencing → risk register.
research: Public data, competitor structure, and unit economics reconstruction from the outside.
discovery: Which side is genuinely constrained, and whether the constraint is supply volume or supply quality.
ux: Not the primary lens — this artefact is deliberately strategic rather than design-led.
metrics: Liquidity rate, time-to-match, take rate, and supply-side retention as the guardrail.
tradeoffs: Subsidising supply buys liquidity and costs margin. The document states the price of each option rather than pretending there is a free one.
risks: Subsidy becomes structural; quality degrades as volume grows.
businessImpact: Strategic recommendation with sized outcomes and explicit kill criteria.
rationale: Ranked #3. Deliberately outside B2B operations — it demonstrates strategic thinking beyond your current domain, which is exactly the Product Strategy gap.

title: Public Product Teardown Series
problem: Your product judgement is invisible to anyone who has not worked with you.
goal: A recurring series analysing Slack, Notion, Linear, Figma and Stripe Dashboard — reconstructing the decisions from the outside.
process: Fixed format per teardown: the constraint the product chose, the data model implied by the UI, and one thing you would change.
research: Hands-on use, changelog archaeology, and public engineering writing.
discovery: What the product refuses to do, and what that refusal buys.
ux: IA and interaction analysis with annotated screens.
metrics: Series-level: reach, inbound conversations, and citations by other PMs.
tradeoffs: A series is a standing commitment. Cadence beats depth; a monthly teardown that ships outranks a perfect one that does not.
risks: Quality drift as novelty fades. Mitigated by the fixed format and a length ceiling.
businessImpact: Distribution and discoverability — the direct fix for "outside your network, almost nobody knows you".
rationale: Ranked #4. Names Slack, Notion, Linear, Figma and Stripe Dashboard specifically. A series compounds where single artefacts do not.

title: Analytics Case Study — Funnel, Retention, Cohorts
problem: A product loses most of its signups before they reach value, and nobody can say precisely where or why.
goal: Find the drop, quantify it, explain it, and recommend three interventions with expected effect sizes.
process: Question framing → funnel analysis → retention curve → cohort comparison → recommendations.
research: A public product dataset, analysed in SQL and in Amplitude.
discovery: The behaviour that separates retained users from churned ones in week one.
ux: Data presentation: every chart carries a sentence saying what to do about it.
metrics: Step conversion, D1/D7/D30 retention, cohort retention curves, and the retention plateau.
tradeoffs: Correlational, not causal, and the write-up says so. Honesty about that limit is itself the signal.
risks: Confusing correlation for cause. Mitigated by naming the experiment that would establish causality.
businessImpact: Three sized recommendations, and the first public proof that you can do analytics.
rationale: Ranked #5, and scheduled earliest deliberately — it is the fastest route from Analytics 6.5 to visible evidence.

title: Product Strategy Memo — Should Company X Enter Market Y?
problem: A company with a strong position in one market is considering an adjacent one, and the decision is being made on enthusiasm.
goal: A memo that reaches a clear recommendation with numbered assumptions, sized risks, and criteria that would prove it wrong.
process: Market sizing → competitive position → where we would win → what would have to be true → recommendation → kill criteria.
research: Public market data, competitor teardown, and stated assumptions where data is unavailable.
discovery: The one assumption the whole recommendation rests on.
ux: Document design: recommendation first, evidence second, appendix third.
metrics: Leading indicators for the first two quarters, and the number that would trigger a stop.
tradeoffs: Entering costs focus in the core market. The memo prices that rather than ignoring it.
risks: Market sizing built on assumptions that do not survive contact. Every one is numbered so it can be checked.
businessImpact: A go/no-go recommendation a real executive could act on.
rationale: Ranked #6. The direct answer to the audit's strategy diagnosis: "should this company even build this?" rather than "how should this product evolve?"

title: Open Source Contribution
problem: Your technical credibility and your collaboration style are both asserted rather than demonstrated.
goal: A merged contribution to a reputable project — documentation, UX improvement, or product planning.
process: Choose the project → find real friction → propose → contribute → get it merged.
research: Issue archaeology to find what maintainers actually want.
discovery: Where new contributors get stuck — usually the highest-value thing to fix.
ux: Documentation IA or an onboarding-flow improvement.
metrics: Merged PRs, and any measurable change in contributor onboarding.
tradeoffs: Documentation contributions merge faster than code; code contributions signal more. Do documentation first to build standing.
risks: Maintainer responsiveness is outside your control. Mitigate by picking an active project.
businessImpact: Public, verifiable, timestamped evidence of collaboration on someone else's terms.
rationale: Ranked #7. The audit specifies documentation, UX improvements or product planning on a reputable project.

title: Enterprise Permissions Model — Case Study
problem: Role-based permissions collapse when real organisations have matrix structures, delegation and temporary access.
goal: Design a permissions model that handles the real cases without becoming a configuration language.
process: Requirements from real org structures → model design → UI for granting and auditing → migration.
research: Five customer org charts and every permissions support ticket from a quarter.
discovery: Administrators do not want power, they want to be able to explain who can see what.
ux: Permission-granting flow, an effective-permissions viewer, and an audit trail.
metrics: Misconfiguration rate, time-to-provision a new user, and permission-related tickets.
tradeoffs: Chose a constrained role model with explicit delegation over full ABAC. Costs expressiveness; buys explicability.
risks: Under-serving the largest customers. Mitigated by an explicit escalation path rather than universal flexibility.
businessImpact: Modelled: 50% reduction in permission misconfiguration incidents.
rationale: Case study #2 for Month 6. Permissions is named in the audit as part of your complex-enterprise-UX advantage — this makes it public.
